In this lesson, you will learn about multivibrators.
INTRODUCTIONM
Multivibrators are circuits that produce square waves.
For example, radar systems use multivibrators to determine how often a pulse will be transmitted.
Computers use multivibrators called flip-flops, to store digital data.
There are many types of multivibrators, but they all operate on the principle that transistors can be either in cutoff or in saturation..

The value of the components in the multivibrator circuit determine the square wave output frequency.
Frequencies range from a few hertz to hundreds of mega hertz.
Multivibrators use two transistor amplifiers.
The transistors are biased so that they are either in cutoff or saturation and never operate between these two points.
When discussing multivibrators, a transistor is said to be ON when in saturation and OFF when in cutoff.
A feedback circuit is added that controls which transistor is ON and which transistor is OFF.

The output is taken from the collector of one of the transistors.
When the transistor is OFF (cutoff), no current flows from emitter to collector. The output voltage is Vcc.
When the transistor is OFF (cutoff), no current flows from collector to emitter. The output voltage is Vcc.
TRANSISTOR IN CUTOFF - When a transistor is in cutoff, it acts like an open circuit. The output voltage is approximately Vcc.
When the transistor is ON (saturation), maximum current flows from emitter to collector. The output voltage is 0.
When the transistor is ON (saturation), maximum current flows from collector to emitter. The output voltage is 0.
When the transistor is ON (saturation), maximum current flows from emitter to collector. The output voltage is 0.
When the transistor is ON (saturation), maximum current flows from collector to emitter. The output voltage is 0.
TRANSISTOR IN SATURATION - When a transistor is in saturation, it acts like a short circuit. All of Vcc is dropped across the collector load resistor.
When the feedback circuit forces Q2 OFF, the output voltage is Vcc or high. This is the positive peak of the square wave.
When the feedback circuit forces Q2 ON, the output voltage is 0 or low. This is the negative peak of the square wave.
The frequency of the output square wave depends on how fast the feedback circuit forces the transistors to switch from ON to OFF.
Component values in the feedback circuit determine the speed of switching.
Note that the output can be on either Q2 or Q1. Normally, multivibrators have connections for both outputs.

There are two general categories of multivibrators.
Free-running multivibrators generate square wave outputs as soon as power is applied.
As long as the DC operating voltage is present, the feedback circuit switches the transistors between ON and OFF.
Triggered multivibrators only produce a square wave output when an external input is applied.
The feedback circuit only switches the transistors between ON and OFF on an input pulse.
Remember, the square wave is produced by the action of a transistor at cutoff and saturation. The feedback circuit controls that action.

MULTIVIBRATOR CIRCUITS
Multivibrators are classified according to the number of stable states that are produced by the feedback circuit.
DISCUSSION
A multivibrator that has no stable state is free running. They are called ASTABLE.
When power is applied, Q1 and Q2 switch back and forth between ON and OFF, no steady state condition.
A multivibrator that has one steady condition is called MONOSTABLE.
When power is applied, Q2 is ON and remains ON (Q1 is OFF). It is a triggered multivibrator.
An input pulse causes Q2 to turn OFF and Q1 to turn ON.
After the input pulse is gone, the multivibrator returns to its one steady state condition, Q2 ON.
A multivibrator that has two steady conditions is called BISTABLE.
When power is applied assume Q2 is ON and remains ON. It is also a triggered multivibrator.
When power is applied, Q1 or Q2 can be ON. However, the operation remains the same...
An input pulse causes Q2 to turn OFF and Q1 to turn ON.
However, after the input pulse is gone, Q1 remains ON. It stays in its second stable state condition.
A second input pulse causes Q1 to turn OFF and Q2 to turn ON.
After the second input pulse is gone, Q2 remains ON. It stays in its first stable state condition.
Determining if a multivibrator is astable, monostable or bistable depends on the components in the feedback circuit.

The type of multivibrator is easily identified by the components used in the feedback circuit.
Let's look at the feedback circuit of an astable multivibrator first. Astable
An astable multivibrator uses two capacitors in the feedback circuit.
The output of Q1 is fed back through one capacitor to the input of Q2.
The output of Q2 is fed back through the other capacitor to the input of Q1...
The charging and discharging of the two capacitors causes the two transistors to continually switch back and forth between ON and OFF.
Next, let's look at a monostable multivibrator feedback circuit.
A monostable multivibrator uses one capacitor and one resistor in the feedback circuit.
The output of Q1 is fed back through the capacitor to the input of Q2.
The output of Q2 is fed back through the resistor to the input of Q1.
The trigger input is applied to the input of Q1.

The charging and discharging of the capacitor on the output of Q1 is coupled to the input of Q2, unless Q1 has an input pulse applied. The resistor on the input of Q2 provides bias voltage to keep Q2 ON..ied.......
Last, let's look at a bistable multivibrator feedback circuit.
A bistable multivibrator uses two capacitors and two resistors in the feedback circuit.
The output of Q1 is fed back through the parallel capacitor and resistor to the input of Q2.
The output of Q2 is fed back through the other parallel capacitor and resistor to the input of Q1.
The trigger input is applied to the inputs of both Q1 and Q2.
The feedback circuit keeps each transistor in one state until an input pulse changes them.
Remember, to identify the type of multivibrator, look at the feedback circuit.
